answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1770–1827 · in a letter of his own hand
answer.sourceLine: Beethoven really wrote this — it comes from his letter to a young admirer, Emilie M., sent from Teplitz on 17 July 1812. The familiar English (“force your way into its secrets … raise men to the divine”) is a faithful but slightly loose translation of his German; a more literal rendering is “penetrate its inner depths … only art and science raise man to the Godhead.”

source.excerpt: Do not merely practice your art, but force your way into its secrets; it deserves that, for only art and science can exalt man to divinity.
trail: Beethoven wrote it in a letter to a little girl, Emilie M., from Teplitz on 17 July 1812 — she had sent him a hand-embroidered pocket-book, and he wrote back with advice on being an artist (The Marginalian).
Wikiquote lists the line in its Sourced section and preserves the German: “dringe auch in ihr Inneres … nur die Kunst und die Wissenschaft erhöhen den Menschen bis zur Gottheit” (Wikiquote).
The exact popular English varies by translator — a modern edition renders it “get at the very heart of it” rather than “force your way into its secrets” (The Marginalian).

The 1909 Kalischer & Shedlock critical edition — the standard English translation, and the one named in the citation above — already contains the letter to “Emilie M. at H.” (Töplitz, 17 July 1812) (Internet Archive).
source.excerptNote: Wikiquote’s sourced wording of the passage; the widely shared version swaps in “knowledge” for “science” and “the divine” for “divinity.”
source.rightsNote: Beethoven’s German original dates to 1812, and every documented English translation of the passage was published well before 1931 — the German appears in Musical News, Vol. 3 (1892), and the standard critical translation is Shedlock & Kalischer’s of 1909. All are in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
author.heading: About Ludwig van Beethoven
author.bio: Ludwig van Beethoven (1770–1827) was a German composer and pianist whose work bridges the Classical and Romantic eras. By 1812, when he wrote to Emilie, he was already losing his hearing yet at the height of his powers. He was a frequent, vivid letter-writer, and this note of encouragement to a child is one of his most quoted.

misattribution.heading: So what's the catch?
misattribution.intro: The author is right — the catch is the wording. This is one of several English translations of a German sentence, and it is almost always posted with no source at all.

items.why: “Force your way into its secrets” and “knowledge” are free renderings of Beethoven’s “dringe auch in ihr Inneres” (penetrate its inner depths) and “Wissenschaft” (science). Other editions read “get at the very heart of it” instead (The Marginalian).
Quote sites typically show the line with no citation at all — Goodreads carries the popular wording flagged as community-added and unverified (Goodreads).

misattribution.truthLine: It is authentic Beethoven, from his letter to Emilie M. of 17 July 1812 — just read it as a translation, and prefer a sourced edition (Wikiquote, Sourced).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In the summer of 1812 an eight-to-ten-year-old girl named Emilie, prompted by her governess, wrote Beethoven a fan letter and sent him a hand-embroidered pocket-book. From Teplitz he wrote back — not with a brush-off but with real counsel: keep at your art, but go deeper than mere practice, because art and knowledge are what lift human beings toward the divine.
The line endures because it captures Beethoven’s own creed — that art is a form of knowing, not just doing — addressed with startling seriousness to a child.
context.pull: “… only art and science raise man to the Godhead.”
